Sources: 252 educational LinkedIn posts by André Luiz Rodrigues (Capital Markets Technology Director; mathematician, ~20 years building pricing and risk systems), pulled from his activity feed on 2026-10-31. The feed held 379 posts: 75 reposts of other authors, 1 duplicate and 51 greetings, certifications and announcements were dropped. Most posts carry a hand-drawn whiteboard with the equations (239 of 252 have a visual). Summarized in own words, not reproduced.

Raw corpus is local-only. His posts and images are his copyrighted work and this repo is public, so the corpus and its reader live in _ingest/raw/2026-10-31/linkedin/andre-rodrigues/, which is gitignored. Open index.html there to read every post with its whiteboard, filtered by topic, problem and party. posts.json holds the same data with tags; build.py regenerates both from feed_raw.json.

Time window: December 2025 to October 2026. Dates are approximate (worked out from LinkedIn's relative "3mo" labels).

Maps to: Course 02 (valuation: discounting and the risk-free curve under every DCF), Course 07 (models, calibration, reading probabilities off prices), Course 11 / E9 (rates, FX, emerging-market plumbing), E2 (capital allocation: funding and capital cost), E6 (crisis: 2008, negative rates, margin spirals), E10 (AI and quantum in a regulated, model-heavy industry).

⚠ Bias. He is a builder of pricing and risk systems, so he frames most problems as model or architecture problems and under-weights incentives, politics and sales. Posts are written for LinkedIn reach: contrarian hooks ("Stop trusting N(d1)", "Stop summing your Vega") overstate the point, which is usually standard practitioner caution. A few posts on quantum computing and AI policy are more enthusiastic than evidenced. The historical failure cases in the map below are added context from this note, not claims from his posts.

What this adds to the program

  • A derivatives layer the repo did not have. wss rates macro covers bond math, DV01 and the curve from a rates salesperson's seat; wss trading hedge funds covers options only as put/call ratios. Nothing in notes/, learn/ or GLOSSARY.md explains how a derivative is priced, risked, hedged and charged for credit and funding. This corpus does, end to end, with the math on a whiteboard.
  • A problem-first index. Topic labels ("options", "rates") say what a post is about. The tags here say what problem it solves and for whom, which is the question an MBA reader actually has.
  • The technologist's view. His recurring claim is that pricing errors come from architecture more often than from math. That is the bridge to bloomberg hub, tradeweb ai price and the vendor economics in the company studies.

The six problems every derivative position creates

Almost every concept he teaches answers one of six questions. They stack: each one assumes the one above it is solved.

# Problem Who has it Concepts (his posts) What goes wrong without it (added context)
P1 Value it. What is this contract worth today? Dealers, funds, auditors, anyone who must mark a book Risk-neutral pricing, discounting, curve building (SOFR, Fed Funds), Black-Scholes as a heat equation, PDE boundary conditions, Monte Carlo, trees No agreed value means no trading, no accounting, no collateral. The LIBOR scandal forced a decade-long rebuild of the curves under ~$300tn of contracts.
P2 Measure the risk. How much do I lose if the market moves? Trading desks, risk managers, regulators Greeks and their failure modes, Taylor expansion of P&L, VaR and the "turkey problem", PCA on curves, Jacobians and gradients as sensitivities, risk attribution Hidden exposure blows up in one day: short-volatility products in Feb 2018; JPMorgan's 2012 "London Whale," where a VaR model change understated risk.
P3 Hedge it. How do I neutralize a risk I don't want to own? Corporates (exporters, importers), funds, the dealers who take the other side Replication and forwards, option strategies as building blocks (spreads, condors, butterflies, diagonals), futures and NDFs, Brazil's synthetic onshore dollar Hedges that are really bets. Sadia and Aracruz lost billions in 2008 on FX structures sold as protection.
P4 Will they pay? What if the other side defaults? Banks with uncollateralized trades, CCPs CVA/DVA and the XVA family, copulas and joint default (Li, Sklar), Poisson default intensities 2008: banks lost more from marking counterparty risk (CVA) than from actual defaults, per the Basel Committee. Archegos (2021) repeated it.
P5 Fund it. Can I carry the position and meet the margin calls? Bank treasury and XVA desks, pension funds, CCPs FVA/MVA/KVA, funding curves, CDI/SELIC/SOFR as funding anchors, settlement conventions, stale pricing in private assets Solvent but illiquid: the 2022 UK pension (LDI) crisis was a margin-call spiral, not a solvency problem.
P6 Compute it. Can the systems produce all of the above fast, consistently and explainably? Bank technology, vendors, fintechs Curve-engine architecture, numerical methods, physics-informed neural networks, neural curve fitting vs. Nelson-Siegel-Svensson, quantum computing Two systems disagree on one trade; an overnight risk run misses its window; nobody can explain a P&L move. When rates went negative, models that assumed log-normal rates (Black-76) stopped producing prices.

How they chain. You cannot hedge (P3) what you cannot measure (P2), and you cannot measure what you cannot value (P1). XVA is what P1 looks like once the clean assumptions fail: it re-prices the trade for P4 (default) and P5 (funding and capital). P6 sits under all of them, because every number above is produced by a system.

Tags are keyword-based and meant as a starting index, not a verdict. 9 posts carry no problem tag.

His series, read as short courses

He posts in sequences. Read in order, each one is a short course on one problem.

Series When Problem What it builds
Math toolkit Jan 2026, Sep 2026 P1, P2, P6 Gradients, Jacobians, Hessians, optimization (gradient descent to metaheuristics), PCA, Taylor expansion, Fourier, Itô, Sklar. The sensitivities in P2 are these derivatives.
Options as building blocks Mar–Apr 2026 P3 Covered call → protective put → verticals → calendars → diagonals → butterflies → condors → double diagonal. Each structure is a different bet on price, time or volatility.
Greeks in practice Mar 2026 P2 Why delta-hedged books still lose, why summing vega across expiries is wrong, gamma near expiry (0DTE), theta as the price of gamma.
Exotics May 2026 P1, P3 Single → double barriers, Asians, TARFs, accumulators, quantos, PRDCs. Path-dependence breaks closed-form pricing, which pushes you into P6.
Curve building Aug 2026 P1, P5, P6 Fed Funds and SOFR curves, risk-free discounting, why curve construction is system design.
Brazil onshore dollar Oct 2026 P3, P5 Why a non-convertible currency forces a separate onshore dollar curve (cupom cambial), and the instruments that trade it (DDI, FRC, NDFs, CDI swaps). How a local bank absorbs an exporter's hedge.
Rates when models break Oct 2026 P1, P6 Negative rates vs. log-normal models, inflation linkers, curve-slope trades and the hedge ratios that keep them direction-neutral.
XVA Oct 2026 (ongoing) P4, P5 Why pre-2008 pricing assumed risk-free funding and safe counterparties; CVA, then DVA and its "phantom profit" paradox.
AI and quantum in finance Dec 2025–Feb 2026, Oct 2026 P6 Transformers and BERT vs. GPT, PINNs that respect no-arbitrage, neural nets vs. parametric curves, quantum algorithms and the encryption threat.

Where the problems are still open (the MBA angle)

P1–P3 are largely solved for large banks; the money and the friction are in P4–P6 and in the under-served parties.

  1. XVA compute cost (P4–P6). XVA needs portfolio-wide Monte Carlo across every counterparty and scenario. Banks spend on GPUs, algorithmic differentiation and neural approximations of slow pricers (his PINN and neural-curve posts). This is the vendor wedge for bloomberg hub-style platforms.
  2. Mid-market corporate hedging (P3). The Brazil series shows a local dealer manufacturing dollar liquidity for an exporter. The exporter usually cannot evaluate what it bought, and 2008 showed the cost. Hedge transparency for mid-size treasurers is an open product problem. See tradeweb derivatives regulation.
  3. Consistency and explainability (P6). Front office, risk and finance often run separate engines that disagree. His "bad architecture, not bad math" claim is the thesis; regulators asking for every number to be explained is the forcing function.
  4. Liquidity under stress (P5). Margin spirals (LDI 2022, March 2020) show funding risk is under-modeled outside large banks. His private-markets post adds the mirror image: smoothed private marks hide volatility until a liquidity event forces a real price (wss private markets wealth).

Suggested reading path

  1. Math toolkit posts, alongside the textbooks: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives, for P1–P3; Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance, for the notation on his whiteboards.
  2. Options as building blocks, then Greeks in practice (P3 → P2).
  3. Curve building, then Rates when models break (P1 at its foundation).
  4. Exotics, then Numerical methods (where P1 forces P6).
  5. XVA with Gregory, The xVA Challenge (P4–P5; his coverage is thin here).
  6. Brazil onshore dollar as a case study of all six problems at once inside one market.
  7. AI and quantum last, as a view on where P6 is heading.

Each step pairs with one buildable exercise for quant-backtesting/ or an Acumen case: a SOFR curve bootstrapper (P1), a Black-Scholes pricer with Greeks and a Taylor P&L explain (P2), a delta-hedging simulation that shows hedge slippage (P3), a barrier option by Monte Carlo vs. PDE (P6), and a one-netting-set CVA (P4). fourier use cases already has a Fourier pricing demo that matches his Fourier posts.

Gaps

  • Counterparty and funding (P4, P5) are thin: 11 and 44 posts. XVA started in October 2026 and is ongoing; re-pull in a few months.
  • No permalinks: the activity feed did not expose links for most posts, so posts are referenced by series and topic, not URL.
  • Images are capped at the sizes LinkedIn served (mostly 1280px, a few at 160–480px).
  • Tags are keyword-based. Spot-checked, not hand-labeled; expect some posts in a neighbouring bucket.
